>

@Jagaraciao:  Give us a TV show, Movie or Book that you love but might be embarrassed to admit it if we knew you in person.
 
Hmmm. Hadn't thought about this before much... I tend to be pretty open and comfortable with my choices of entertainment... but one incident does come to mind. 
When I first came to the US I was about 9 years old and I didn't speak any English. I remember struggling at first at school trying to figure out what people were saying. As my language skills began to develop I took to read Ung everything I could get my hands on. It was much easier than speaking to people since I could do it at my own pace and I didn't have to worry about butchering pronounciation (How did the English language get "won" out of o-n-e?). 
Anyhow, in the house I was staying in at the time I found a box full of old books from the previous owner and out if all of them the only ones I could really relate to at that age were an almost complete collection of "The Babysitter Club". I read them all. They were really a key part if my formative English-speaking years and as such held a bit of a sentimentl value... so I kept them even as I grew older. 
One day in late high school, a bunch of friends were over at my place to work on a group project... and while I was searching for something or another (can't remember what it was) I knocked down a box from my closet and out spilled my collection of "The Babysitters Club". I was just about to play it off and claim they were my sister's old books (even though they were clearly in a box with other stuff of mine), when as if on cue, in walks my sister and says "Eww whose girlie books are there?"
So yeah, I was mortified, hahaha.

jagarciao:

@BlueHairedMeerkat:  You are a bartender working an event at the Freedom Five Tower where all the heroes are attending. Who are the first five to walk up to the bar and what do they order? 

First to the bar is Tachyon, who orders six bags of chips and a bottle of water, before shooting off to do… something or other. She doesn't stay at the event, anyway, but instead heads for the stairs. Second up is a sulky Unity, who orders a strawberry daquiri (just because of the name, probably) and sits on a barstool, stirring it glumly, while telling me about how Tachy's doing some kind of experiment (she mentioned some details, but they went right over my head) and how it's super-exciting but Unity isn't allowed to help. Third is Legacy, who takes Unity's daquiri away, admonishes her for drinking ("I'm 19!" she protests), and orders a cola and a glass of white wine; the latter is for Mrs Parsons and the former for an increasingly despondent Unity.

Fourth is Lt. Vance, who orders a beer and takes a seat next to Unity. From their conversation, I glean that he's not particularly happy either; he always feels out of place at these community events, but as a member of the Freedom Five he's practically obliged to put in an appearance. The two spend a little time complaining at each other before person number five, a recently-materialised Chrono-Ranger (who has alarmed quite a few people by appearing so suddenly, but doesn't seem to care), who orders Vance to start evacuating the building, because things are about to go very, very wrong. Tyler Vance tries to hide the gleam in his eyes as he leaps up and begins to do as the cowboy commands; Unity grins as she gazes up at a nearby wall-mounted television, and begins to transform it…

It's about then that the screaming starts.

Hmm, ninja clan? Okay…so not knowing many specifics about actual ninjas, I'll just base this on what I've seen in anything that features ninjas ;). Right then, so my clan would be all dark and stealthy. We can blend into any shadow and avoid detection. We live in some secret place somewhere…a forest, yeah, that'll do, where all the trees are big and their branches are wonderfully strong and twisty, so we can climb through them with ease and have lots of little nooks and dens up there, as well as various little hideouts scattered across the forest floor, and some kind of means of keeping in contact with each other as one big network. When in the forest, we know the behaviour of the local wildlife so well that we can easily imitate the movements and sounds to fool passers-by into thinking that we're just some random harmless creature rustling in the bushes, if we choose to make any noise at all. Some of our members travel around and visit towns and cities and stuff, and keep an eye out for people who are basically cruel, spiteful, greedy, etc. Because those people deserve to be taught a lesson in how to be considerate to other people. So we will leave them a warning of some kind…maybe one of our members will (in disguise, of course, as someone the person being approached wouldn't see as suspicious and would be willing to talk to), approach them and initiate a casual conversation, at some point slipping in a suggestion that perhaps they should change their behaviour and treat people better because otherwise it might bite them on the bum later. And if they don't heed this subtle warning, then we sneak in and yoink all their money or otherwise disable whatever bad things they've been doing (eg if they're some corrupt ruler who's been locking innocent people up for no reason, we'll go and break open the prison). We use our imitation skills and general Sneaky Bastard Tactics to carry out our objectives, preferably without hurting anyone and certainly not leaving a corpse trail. We'll be sort of like a gang of ninja Robin Hoods, I suppose, but people won't ever know who we are or where we live because we stay incognito the whole time. Something like that, anyway.

My house is on a quiet cul-de-sac and contains me, my boyfriend, an old Labrador called Summer, a Netherland Dwarf rabbit called Neo (no, not named after Keanu Reeves in The Matrix), hundreds of pieces of jewellery, a small studio room full of art and craft stuff where I make said jewellery, hundreds of balls of yarn, many crocheted amigurumi animals and superheroes, about 140 board games, thousands of books, a collection of over 2000 can ring pulls from when I was a teenager, two shelves full of old RPG systems, a cider apple press, a cupboard full of different kinds of caffeine-free tea, an electric drum kit and various plastic instruments to play Rock Band, a shelving unit full of glue and card and paper and sticky-backed plastic and blank dice and tokens and tiles for PnP games, about 50 different herbs and spices, and a desktop computer which has a vital role of allowing me to play Skyrim, The Sims 2 and 3, Minecraft and more importantly Sentinels via G+. Oh and a lot of stuff we don't want which we're slowly throwing out/selling/giving away. 

What's it like? Currently messy and disorganised but gradually getting less so. And the awesomeness level is soon to go up with the imminent arrival of Vengeance, and with it the compulsion to crochet 8 new heroes.

posts.cooked:
Oh, good one...

 

If it's ok, I'm going to go with an 11-way tie.

 

Well, actually a 2-way tie between a single book, House of the Scorpion, by Nancy Farmer, and a 10-book series, The Pendragon Adventures, by DJ MacHale. (My first instinct was to bring up the Song of Ice and Fire, but of course just about everyone's heard of Game of Thrones by now, what with the TV show and all, and it had to be an obscure one.)

 

I last read House of the Scorpion a LONG time ago, so I'm really fuzzy on the exact details of the plot, but it takes place in a dystopian future in the nation of Opium; basically a massive poppy field growing along the border of USA and Mexico. The main character, Matt, is a clone of this really old drug lord (or something like that; basically, the MOST RICH JERKASS) raised specifically with the intent of being harvested for spare parts. He escapes into Mexico, and finds his way into and out of various entrapments of different types, while constantly having to hide the PROPERTY OF MATTEO whateverhisnamewas tattoo that marks him as a clone, and therefore less than human. Less valuable even than the eejits, mind-wiped slaves that could obey simple commands but had absolutely no decision-making ability of their own; if you told them to drink, they would keep drinking until their stomachs explodes, and then keep going until they died, or you told them to stop. It's a really moving, deep introspective on the meaning of humanity and all that. Plus, it gave me one of my favorite quotes, and my personal philosophy on life: "Arguing isn't bad, it's actually good for you. It's like doing pushups with your mind."

(Also, looking on wikipedia, there was apparently a sequel that was released September of LAST YEAR. So I'll have to get to reading THAT.)

 

The Pendragon Adventures, on the other hand, is much less... heartwrenching. (Well, for the most part.) It's a medium-light sci-fi/fantasy series about Bobby Pendragon, who is eventually revealed to be a part of a specially chosen group of people called Travelers; people with the ability to utilize the pathways between worlds -- or Territories, as they're called -- to travel between them, jumping through space and time in order to save everything; all of time and space, that ever was and will be (collectivelly called Halla) from Saint Dane, a corrupted Traveler who wants nothing more than to cause chaos and destruction. What makes it unique, among other things, is the format. The story alternates between traditionally-narrated segments in the 21st century (Second Earth, in Territory terms. Yes, there are a First and Third Earth.) following Bobby's friends, Mark and Courtney, and Bobby's segments, which are delivered in the forms of journals, written by Bobby and read by Mark and Courtney. The contrast between Bobby's fantastic adventures and his friends' more-or-less ordinary life is really well-illustrated and realistic, the different worlds he visits are all unique and entertaining (and some are quite frightening, for various reasons; most for psychological reasons. For instance, consider: what if Wal-Mart took over the world?), the conflicts on the individual worlds are unique and engaging, and they all tie in to a longer over-arching narrative that gets progressively shocking and unpredictable, without feeling forced or cliched. Also, they're hilarious; MacHale's comedic timing is PERFECT. He knows exactly how to write people.

If you want to read them, the books are:

The Merchant of Death

The Lost City of Faar

The Never War

The Reality Bug

Black Water

The Rivers of Zadaa

The Quillan Games

The Pilgrims of Rayne

Raven Rise

Soldiers of Halla
